newsitem.title: USA: NHL ICE HOCKEY - FEDOROV SHINES IN RED WINGS' MARCH TO CUP.
newsitem.headline: NHL ICE HOCKEY - FEDOROV SHINES IN RED WINGS' MARCH TO CUP.

text.p: Sergei Fedorov, once railed as a graceful skater who wasn't tough enough for the bruising NHL playoffs, left little doubt Thursday night about his desire to win the Stanley Cup.

Fedorov, star of Detroit's "Russian Five" -- all former members of the Soviet Central Red Army team -- scored two goals and set up two more in the Red Wings' 6-1 total domination of the Philadelphia Flyers that gave them a near insurmountable 3-0 lead in the best-of-seven championship series.
"I feel great to win game number three. I was a little nervous," he admitted.

About the prospect of bringing Detroit it's first Stanley Cup since 1955 Fedorov said: "It's going to be unbelievable for us and for all the people in Detroit, Michigan, but we've got one more game to play, we're going to try and focus on that game."

So far, focus has not been a problem for Fedorov, who has scored eight goals in the playoffs -- three in the finals -- compared just two in 1996, when Detroit was favoured to win the Stanley Cup but fell to the evental champion Colorado Avanlanche in the semifinals.

On his first goal Thursday night, the swift skating centre displayed the type of moves that made him famous -- a steal of the puck at the blue line, a breakaway and a quick, deft move for the kill that left Flyers goalie Ron Hextall handcuffed.
"I can't give everything to myself, but I feel pretty good what I am doing," he said after the victory. "I think I am playing pretty well and best hockey I have ever played."
The rap against the Russian players had been that they just didn't have the hunger for the Stanley Cup that the league's Canadians had dreamed about all their lives.
Olymic gold yes, but the Russians did not seem willing to lay it all on the line when other were sacrificing their bodies in the quest for the Cup.
But Fedorov and his compatriots have learned a few hard lessons.

A stunning first-round loss in 1994, Detroit's 1995 Stanley Cup finals sweep by the New Jersey Devils and last year's elimination by the Avalanche following a record 62-victory season humbled him and the rest of the Red Wings.
He know's Philadelphia's pain.
"I think it is pretty hard to think what Flyers see or going through because we have got so much emotion going on our bench," Fedorov said in his Russian-accented English.
"We have been through a lot last couple of three years, but you know, again, most important thing (is to) concentrate on our game, how important it is for us and what we have to do next."
Like the rest of the Wings, he also has adopted a much more defensive style of play.
That manifested itself in the first period Thursday when he helped successfully kill a five-on-three penalty situation, which he said was a major turning point for the Red Wings.

He has been playing for several years with most of the team's Russians -- Vladimir Konstantinov, Slava Fetisov, Slava Kozlov and Igor Larionov -- and said they have gelled together well with the rest of the team.
In fact, Detroit is 14-0 in the playoffs this year when at least one member of the free-wheeling Russian unit has scored a goal.
"When you communicate with your teammates, you have lots of support, you can give lots of support.
"That is what gives you composure and give you that feeling when you really on your stride -- big stride."
